title: Why Did Moses Resist God's Calling?
paragraphs:
Why Did Moses Resist God's Calling?
The Five Words That Almost Changed History Forever—and the Grace That Still Pursues the Reluctant Heart
There are moments in life when the greatest danger is not failure.
It is saying "no" to the very God who created you.
But because you honestly believe someone else would do a better job.
Perhaps that is exactly where you are today.
You pray, but secretly believe your past has disqualified you.
You attend church but feel invisible.
You read Scripture yet cannot imagine God using someone like you.
You smile in public while carrying private shame.
You love Jesus—but you struggle to believe He truly wants you.
If that is your story, then Moses is about to become more than a Bible character.
Because one of the greatest leaders in history almost walked away from the calling of God—not out of rebellion, but out of fear.
And if grace had not pursued him, Israel's story might have looked very different.
That is why the story of Moses is ultimately not about the courage of a man.
It is about the relentless mercy of a Savior who refuses to abandon hesitant people.
It is another beautiful reminder of our theme:
Long before Moses stood before Pharaoh, before the Red Sea split, before Mount Sinai shook with the glory of God, Moses was hiding in Midian.
Forty years earlier he had lived in Pharaoh's palace.
In anger he murdered an Egyptian.
When his crime became known, Moses fled.
The future deliverer became an anonymous shepherd.
Imagine carrying the weight of one terrible decision for four decades.
Many people today know exactly what that feels like.
A bush burned without being consumed.
Vayera mal'akh YHWH elav belabbat esh
"The Angel of the LORD appeared to him in a flame of fire." (Exodus 3:2)
A perfect picture of God's holiness meeting broken humanity without immediately consuming it.
Then came the words that changed history.
The first objection came from insecurity.
That is exactly where insecurity always begins.
Our eyes leave God and become fixed upon ourselves.
God did not answer Moses with greater confidence.
He answered him with greater presence.
Our culture tells us to believe in ourselves.
Believe the God who walks with you.
Then came one of the greatest revelations in all Scripture.
The Hebrew verb היה (hayah) means "to be."
God is not merely introducing Himself.
He is declaring absolute, eternal existence.
Centuries later Jesus deliberately echoed this divine name.
That is why they picked up stones.
Jesus was identifying Himself with the eternal God revealed to Moses.
The burning bush ultimately points beyond Sinai.
Then came perhaps the objection that resonates most deeply with ordinary people.
"I am not a man of words." (Exodus 4:10)
Some scholars believe Moses struggled with speech.
Others believe he simply lacked confidence.
Either way, God answered with breathtaking simplicity.
God was gently reminding Moses that the One who created his weakness already knew about it before calling him.
God has never accidentally called an imperfect servant.
Your limitations are never a surprise to the Creator.
Finally he uttered five heartbreaking Hebrew words.
This may be one of the most relatable prayers in all the Bible.
How many believers have silently prayed the same words?
Someone whose past isn't as broken as mine.
Exodus tells us that God's anger burned against Moses.
Yet notice what He did next.
But God did not abandon Moses.
This is the rhythm of divine love throughout Scripture.
God refuses to lower His holy standards.
Yet He also refuses to stop pursuing broken people.
Centuries later we meet another reluctant servant.
Yet beside another fire—the charcoal fire on the shore of Galilee—Jesus restored him.
Notice what Jesus did not ask.
The same grace that pursued Moses pursued Peter.
And that same grace pursues us today.
The Gospel is filled with people who believed they were finished.
A Samaritan woman with five failed relationships.
A tax collector despised by his neighbors.
A thief dying on a cross.
Each discovered that Jesus rewrites everything.
That is why Moses' story ultimately belongs to Christ.
Moses led Israel out of slavery in Egypt.
Jesus leads humanity out of slavery to sin.
Jesus eternally intercedes for His people.
Jesus established the new covenant through His blood.
Perhaps you have resisted God's calling for years.
But because you cannot imagine He still wants you.
Maybe your past whispers louder than His promises.
Maybe shame has become your identity.
Maybe fear has disguised itself as humility.
God already knows everything about you.
He knew every sin before calling you.
Grace meets truth with a cross.
That cross stood where justice and mercy embraced.
There the holy God judged sin completely while opening His arms completely to sinners who repent and believe.
Not that good people found God.
But that God pursued broken people through Jesus Christ.
Maybe today you have been saying,
What if Heaven is still answering,
Not because your story is clean.
Scandal does not have the final word.

You never know who may encounter the Gospel because you chose to make Christ visible in your corner of the world. A single share can become an instrument through which God calls another reluctant heart home.
Sometimes the invitation God uses is as simple as a name mentioned in love.
Return to it whenever you are tempted to believe your failures are greater than God's grace.
One surrendered "yes" to Jesus can rewrite generations.
